source.note: Published Listening Comprehension Script from the owner-authorized source book.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Did you buy your ticket from a travel agent or from the airline?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Does it matter? They’re all the same price.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: When do you think your apples will be ready to pick?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You can always tell whether an apple’s ripe by its color.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: My lease is about to expire and I’ve decided to get a larger place. Do you know of any two-bedroom apartments for rent?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Have you checked the off-campus listings at the housing office?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Judy looks terrific these days, better than I’ve ever seen.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I think it’s her new haircut. Short hair really flatters her.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: How about if I come over to pick you up at 6:45 for the movie?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Make it 7. I won’t have finished with dinner until then.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’m moving next week and I have so much to do. I’ll never get it all done.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Don’t forget to tell the post office to forward your mail. You don’t want to miss any important letters.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Is that a new pair of glasses?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’m making do with this old pair until my good ones are fixed.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’ve spent the whole morning at the library…looking for the information we need – you know – for the assignment that’s due Friday?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I’m stuck, too. Maybe Dr. Boyd will have some suggestions.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I thought you wanted orange juice.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: The machine only had milk.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Not many people know that I’m going to get this promotion.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Your secret is safe with me.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: The weather’s so nice, I think I’m going to eat my lunch outside. Care to join me?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’m meeting Bill in the cafeteria at noon. How about tomorrow?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Listen, Eleanor, I shouldn’t have [ shouldn’t’ve] said what I said yesterday. It just didn’t come out right.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, I shouldn’t have [shouldn’t’ve] let it get to me.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Are you just about finished? I need to get ahold of George before we leave.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Just one more quick call, then it’s all yours.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I can’t decide whether to take Professor Brown’s class or Professor Thomson’s.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I can tell you this about Thomson: she knows how to get your attention and hold it.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I heard you were worried about your history final. How did it go?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, the essay part was about what I expected. But the multiple- choice section wasn’t bad – I was really surprised.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You’ve been sitting at that desk for three hours!

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: In half an hour I’m going to take a break for lunch.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I thought you didn’t have time to go to the bank.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It was close, but I made it.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Could you please check the list again? I sent in my registration application and fees for the conference last month.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Let me…oh, you did. Yes, here’s your name. O.K. You can go ahead to the next table for your information kit.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: How do I get to the museum café?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: What does the woman mean?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I’d be glad to drop you off downtown on my way home.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Well…if you’re sure it’s not out of your way.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I’ve got to go to the dentist tomorrow at three. Do you think I could make up the hours I’ll miss another day?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’ll see what I can do.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I can’t seem to shake this cold.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Sometimes the only thing that helps is taking it easy.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I forgot to get a new pen for tomorrow’s calligraphy class. Do you know when the campus store opens in the morning?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I’d try the mall tonight – your class starts early.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I just tried Richard’s house and nobody answered.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That’s odd. He left here at noon, so he should’ve arrived at least 30 minutes ago.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That little grocery store on the corner looks as though it’s seen better days.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I’m afraid it’s only a matter of time before it closes down.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I can’t seem to get the TV to come on. It must be broken.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Have you checked to see if it’s plugged in?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I’d like to get a chair with wheels because I need to be able to get from the computer to the phone more easily.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’ll take it up with Gary in office furnishings, but I can’t make any promises.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: So you think your supervisor approves of your work?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: She didn’t come right out and pat me on the back, but I did get that impression.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Are we all set for the meeting downstairs? I told them we’d need a slide projector…

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I took care of it on my way back from lunch.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Do you think the blue jacket would look better with these pants?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: In this heat, I don’t think you’ll be comfortable in anything but the cotton one.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Good morning, Steve. What can I do for you?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Well, I’ve decided I want to transfer to a smaller college.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I know you’ve had a rough time adjusting, Steve, but I’m sorry to hear you want to leave.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: What I need to do now is find a new college and I was hoping you might have some ideas.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I might, but first I think I ought to warn you about some of the potential problems with transferring. The main one is how many of your credits will be accepted by your new college.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: You mean they won’t all be transferable?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Not necessarily. It’ll depend on what courses you’ve taken here and how they fit in with the requirements at the other school. So whatever college you choose, be sure to find out about transferring your credits.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Who would I talk to about something like that?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: First check with the admissions officer, then follow up with the registrar’s office. Now…the other thing I wanted to caution you about is thinking that a transfer will solve all your problems.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’m not sure I understand what you mean.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, I know you haven’t been happy this semester, but are you sure changing colleges is going to be the answer?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Uhh…I like my classes, except for composition. The math department is everything I expected it to be, but…maybe if my roommate and I had hit it off better…that’s really bothering me more than anything else.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Really? Did you talk to someone at the residence office? It might be that changing roommates would make all the difference.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I might just do that!

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Diane, first let me congratulate you on your latest thriller’s success. Tales of Deception has topped the best-seller list for the past twenty-seven weeks straight. How do you do it?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: In my novels, plot is everything. I am fascinated by suspense, and I try to weave as chilling a tale as possible. I seek to give my readers an extremely intricate mystery that keeps them guessing until the last minute.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: For your latest novel, I understand you worked undercover with the Los Angeles police for several months. What did you get out of that?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, since my main character is a police detective, I needed to immerse myself in that role – to find out how an officer thinks, and how a crime is investigated.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: In addition to telling a powerful story, you are quite deft with language. You seem to place quite an emphasis on precise descriptions, and, of course, you really know how to set the scene.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Thank you. Actually, I began my writing career as a poet. It’s no coincidence that I strive for a certain style.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: It seems to me it would take years to produce something so well written and researched, not to mention the time it takes to work out the plot. And yet, you write so fast that sometimes you’ve got two new books out at the same time. Tell me about your work habits.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I keep at it all the time. I get up at six every morning, review the outline for the chapter I’ll write that day, and don’t stop till I’m finished, sometimes four or five in the afternoon. Even when I’m not at my desk, I’m working. Ideas flash through my mind all day long. That’s why I carry a little notebook around with me.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I guess that’s about all the time we have today. Thanks very much for being with us.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You’re quite welcome.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: As we head into hurricane season, we’d like to take this opportunity to go over some precautionary measures you can take in this dangerous season. This is especially important for those of you living in coastal areas where hurricanes can be destructive because of their heavy winds. The following guidelines have been established by the National Weather Service. Before hurricane season even begins, stock up on batteries, candles, bottled water, nonperishable food such as canned goods, and other emergency equipment. In case of a hurricane warning, following these safety guidelines may help save your life and property. First of all, protect windows with boards or tape, since they’re not strong enough to withstand hurricane-force winds – these winds can reach up to 200 miles per hour! Also the National Weather Service recommends that you fill up your car with fuel in case you need to evacuate. Gas stations may be closed by the time you need to leave your home. Remember also, it is suggested that you stay indoors if your home is sturdy and on high ground. However, homes in low-lying areas will likely be evacuated, since flooding is a possibility. Listen to the radio for emergency weather reports and evacuation information. If called to evacuate, leave the area immediately. You will be advised of the locations of local shelters.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: In the days before telephones, radio, and television, the only network of public communication that could reach farmers was the mail. But this wasn’t the mail as we know it today. At that time, in the early nineteenth century, mail delivery was uneven and widely scattered. In fact, many people living in rural areas got no mail at all. In the early decades of the century, mail carriers were privately employed – they did not work for the government. Many years later, when the government finally took charge of delivering mail, it was mostly in cities that mail got delivered to people’s homes. So farmers still had a problem – they had to go to a post office to collect their mail, which, by the way, wasn’t always nearby. Farmers’ requests to have mail brought to their homes were at first met with outrage. What could be more ridiculous, many urban residents asked, than paying government employees to travel miles across the countryside with an occasional letter? Nevertheless, farmers’ organizations succeeded in convincing the United States Congress that farmers needed mail delivery. Finally in 1891 rural free delivery, known as RFD, came into being. In a sense, rural free delivery was the most important communications revolution in United States history. Rural Americans were not lifted out of the relatively isolated communities they lived in. Because of rural free delivery, there now ran a highway to the world from every farmer’s doorstep.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Today I’d like to explain the Mohs’ scale, used in what is called the “scratch test.” This scale is based on the simple fact that harder minerals scratch softer ones. For example, a diamond; a quartz crystal can scratch a feldspar crystal, but not the other around. The scale is named for Friedrich Mohs, the mineralogist who devised it in 1812. His scale spans the range of minerals known at that time, from the softest to the hardest. By performing a scratch test using known minerals and a few common tools, an unidentified mineral sample can be placed between two points on the scale. By referring to the scale, the mineral can then be identified. I have here a collection of the minerals included on the Mohs’ scale, as well as the tools necessary to complete this exercise. I’d like you each to take a mineral sample from the basket at the front of the room and classify it according to its place on the Mohs’ scale. First, however, I should give you a little warning. The hardness of any mineral depends on the strength of the bonds between ions or between atoms – the stronger the bond, the harder the mineral. Because bond strength may differ in various angles of a crystal, the hardness may vary slightly depending on the direction in which the mineral sample is scratched, so be sure to scratch each sample in several different directions.
